name: Hassan Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Hassan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a leased panel van, doing same-day parcel jobs on three apps, plus direct runs for two hardware stores that call me when a builder needs timber or tiles on site by noon. I'm up at six, and the first thing I do is ask my AI assistant to sort the day's jobs into a route and draft the invoices for yesterday. I've only been driving for myself a year and a half, after leaving a warehouse job, and I still underquote big jobs. I live with my partner Maja, who works at a dental surgery, and we're getting married in the spring.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Loading wears me out, and builders who aren't on site when they said they'd be. What I like is that it's mine. My dad was a builder and always said work for yourself if you can, and now I'm doing it. Every new hardware store that calls me feels like a small win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I'll keep using the bits that work. I'd tell other drivers which AI tools are worth it for invoices and routes. I'd say people should stop waiting for magic and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. My business grows by word of mouth with builders, and AI already saves me an hour a day on paperwork. If nothing big changes, I just keep growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to sign a third hardware store this year and cut down to two apps. Next year I'd look at leasing a second van and taking on a driver for the store runs. I'd keep about four months of savings as my safety net and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Confident, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leasing a second van is a commitment. What if the work dries up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I hand it back early and pay the fee. I've done the numbers with the AI: three good months covers that. I'd rather try and fail than wonder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Piotr, who's nineteen and just finished school. I'd teach him the routes. Family first, and he'd learn a proper way of working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for small businesses who move fast. I'd tell other drivers to use AI for quotes and paperwork. And I'd say the government should get out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this suits me. My driving is hands-on, robots are slow, and AI makes my office side faster. A one-man firm can look like a bigger firm now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get an AI booking system so builders can order a run by text at any hour. I'd lease the second van in the first year. I'd learn whatever new tools come along, quickly, because that's my edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. Like a door's opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses out in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office people, probably, and drivers who just do apps and nothing else. I feel for them, but I'd say learn a trade or build something. My dad didn't wait for anyone to help him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big apps could undercut me with cheaper same-day deals. But builders like a guy they can ring who knows the site. I'd bet on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a big change and people need to get moving now. I'd say businesses that adapt will survive. I wouldn't say the government should fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's bad for my plan. By 2028 the thinking AI does my quotes and booking, which is fine, but by 2031 robot vans can do the runs, and big companies will own them. My little firm wouldn't survive that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't lease the second van; I'd keep the cash. I'd start learning how robot vans are serviced and set up, maybe a course at the college, so I'm the one fixing them. I'd still get married in spring, but we'd keep the house plans on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be lying if I said it didn't worry me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Maja?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Maja the second van is off and we rent for longer. She'd be fine, she's practical. Her dental surgery job is steadier than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you buy a robot van yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if they're leased like vans now. But I'd be competing with giants on price. I'd only do it if I found a niche, like building sites, where the robot needs a person to sort the mess.

S2.quote: By 2031 robot vans can do the runs, and big companies will own them.
fieldNote: He quickly **drops expansion** once robots arrive within three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now. I'd tell drivers to learn a skill around the new machines. I'd say families should plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is decent for me. I'd grow the firm for three years, then lease robot vans myself around 2034 and focus on building sites, where things are messy. I'd be thirty-five and running something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lease the second van in year one and hire Piotr. I'd learn everything about robot vans as they're tested. By year four I'd plan to swap a van for a robot one, if the numbers work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Piotr when you switch to a robot van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train him to supervise and load, and fix the small stuff. I'd be honest with him from the start. He's family, so I wouldn't just drop him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the big firms get there first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd sell them my builders. A list of fifty building sites and the people who run them is worth something. Either way, I'd come out with something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone who wants to build something. I'd tell young people to start a business or learn a trade. I'd say families should back each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is great for me. I could build the firm to three or four vans, then move it onto robots before 2039. I'd be thirty-nine and running a proper firm, maybe with my kids around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the firm, marry Maja, buy a small house in five years. I'd keep learning the new tools as they come. Around year eight I'd start leasing robot vans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say, build it with your hands while you can, then let the machines carry the weight. He'd be proud, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that could still trip you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a big company takes over all same-day deliveries for builders. I'd keep my prices fair and my service personal, and hope that's enough.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time to grow before the robots come. What would help is fair rules so small firms can lease robot vans too, not just the giants. I don't want handouts. I want a fair chance to compete.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about small firms like mine. People think of drivers as app workers, but some of us are building something. We'd need fair access to the new machines.

headlineQuote: I don't want handouts. I want a fair chance to compete.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old** van driver running his own small same-day business for builders.
He uses **AI daily** for routes, quotes and invoices, and likes risk.
He's **traditional**: values family, self-reliance and his builder dad's advice.
He's **calm** in the slow pictures and anxious when robots arrive by 2031.
He plans to **own robot vans** rather than be replaced by them.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to grow before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: Fair rules so **small firms** can lease robot vans too.
